# Install Positron {#sec-positron}

## Overview

::: {.callout-note collapse="false" title="The task: one place to write, run, and render"}

The walkthroughs in this book are Quarto documents that run R, and later Python. You
need a program in which to open them, run their code, and render them.
[Positron](https://positron.posit.co/) is a free editor from Posit, the company that
makes RStudio. It runs R and Python side by side and works with Quarto, so the same
steps apply whichever language a chapter uses.

By the end of this chapter, you will be able to:

1. Install Positron, R, and Quarto, and decide how to install Python.
2. Open a project folder and find the console, the terminal, and the interpreter
   picker.
3. Tell the **console** apart from the **terminal**, which matters for every command
   in the next chapter.

You can follow the book in RStudio or another editor instead. The R code is the same;
only the menus differ.

:::

## Step 1: Download and install Positron

::: {.callout-note collapse="false" title="Pick the installer for your computer"}

Download the installer from <https://positron.posit.co/download.html>.

| Computer | What Positron needs | Installer |
|---|---|---|
| Mac | macOS 11 or later | `.dmg` for Apple Silicon (M-series) or for Intel |
| Windows | Windows 10 or later (Windows 11 on ARM) | `.exe`; choose the user install unless you administer the computer |
| Linux | Ubuntu 20 or later, or Red Hat Enterprise Linux 9 | `.deb` or `.rpm` |

On a Mac, open the `.dmg` and drag Positron to the Applications folder. On Windows, run
the `.exe`; Positron's download page also asks you to have the latest Visual C++
Redistributable installed. Positron checks for its own updates after that.

To find out which Mac you have, open the Apple menu and choose **About This Mac**. A
chip named "Apple M1" (or M2, M3, and so on) means Apple Silicon.

:::

## Step 2: Install R, Quarto, and (when you need it) Python

::: {.callout-note collapse="false" title="Positron runs your code; it does not include the languages"}

Positron starts without any programming language installed, but it cannot run a
chapter until it finds one.

| Software | Needed for | Where to get it |
|---|---|---|
| R 4.2 or later | Every current chapter | <https://cran.r-project.org/> |
| Quarto | Rendering the book | <https://quarto.org/docs/get-started/> |
| Python | Python examples only | Let **uv** or **pixi** install it (next chapter) |

**R.** Install the current release from CRAN. Positron supports R 4.2 and later and
finds R in the standard locations on its own. This book's package versions were
recorded with R 4.6.2.

**Quarto.** Positron ships with Quarto, so previewing a document inside Positron works
without a separate download. Install Quarto yourself as well, so that the `quarto`
command also works in any terminal; the commands in this book assume it does.

**Python.** You do not need to install Python by hand. The tools in the next chapter
download the version a project asks for and keep it with that project.

:::

## Step 3: Open a project folder

::: {.callout-note collapse="false" title="A project is a folder"}

For this walkthrough, open a single project folder. Use **File > Open Folder...** and choose the
folder that holds your project. For this book, that is the folder containing
`_quarto.yml`.

Opening the folder, and not a single file inside it, matters for two reasons. File
paths in the chapters, such as `data/raw/participants.csv`, are written from that
folder. And Positron looks in the open folder for a project environment, which is how
it finds the right R packages and the right Python.

Four parts of the window come up throughout the book:

| Part | Where | What it is for |
|---|---|---|
| Editor | Centre | Open and edit `.qmd`, `.R`, and `.py` files. |
| Console | Bottom | Run R or Python one line at a time and see the result. |
| Terminal | Bottom, next to the console | Run commands for your computer, such as `quarto render`. |
| Interpreter picker | Top right | Shows which R or Python is running, and starts another. |

The **Command Palette** searches every Positron command by name. Open it with
`Cmd+Shift+P` on a Mac or `Ctrl+Shift+P` on Windows and Linux.

:::

## Step 4: Console or terminal?

::: {.callout-note collapse="false" title="Two prompts that accept different commands"}

Beginners often type a command into the wrong one of these, so check before you press
Enter.

| | Console | Terminal |
|---|---|---|
| Talks to | R or Python | Your computer's shell |
| Prompt looks like | `>` for R, `>>>` for Python | A folder name, then `%`, `$`, or `>` |
| Example | `renv::status()` | `quarto render` |

In this book, a block labelled R goes in the R console:

```{.r}
renv::status()
```

A block labelled Bash goes in the terminal. Open one with **Terminal > New Terminal**:

```{.bash}
quarto --version
```

If the terminal prints a version number, Quarto is installed and on your path.

:::

## Step 5: Choose the interpreter

::: {.callout-note collapse="false" title="Which R, which Python"}

The interpreter picker at the top right names the R or Python session that the console
is using. Click it and choose **New Console Session...** to start a different one, or
run **Interpreter: Start New Console Session** from the Command Palette. You can keep
an R session and a Python session open together and switch between them.

When the open folder contains a project environment, the session you want is the one
that belongs to it:

- For R, start R as usual. A project that uses renv switches R to the project's own
  package library as R starts, and the console says so.
- For Python, choose the interpreter whose path is inside the project folder, such as
  `.venv`.

The next chapter sets up those environments.

:::

## Step 6: Render a Quarto document

::: {.callout-note collapse="false" title="From source to page"}

Open a `.qmd` file and use the **Preview** button above the editor to render it and
show the result beside your code. The terminal does the same for a whole book. From
the book's folder:

```{.bash}
quarto preview
```

`quarto preview` rebuilds the page as you save. `quarto render` builds everything once
and writes the result to `_book/`.

Quarto runs R chunks with the R it finds for the project and Python chunks with the
Python it finds. Making sure it finds the project's own copies is the subject of the
next chapter.

:::

## Practice

::: {.callout-note collapse="false" title="Check your setup"}

1. In which pane would you type `quarto render`? In which would you type
   `nrow(mtcars)`?
2. You opened `chapters/data-preparation.qmd` by double-clicking it, and
   `read.csv("data/raw/participants.csv")` fails with "No such file or directory".
   What is the likely cause?
3. How can you tell which version of R the console is running?

:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Suggested answers"}

**1.** `quarto render` is a command for your computer, so it goes in the terminal.
`nrow(mtcars)` is R code, so it goes in the R console.

**2.** Positron opened the file without opening the project folder, so R started
somewhere else and the path does not lead to the data. Use **File > Open Folder...**
and choose the folder containing `_quarto.yml`.

**3.** The interpreter picker at the top right names the session and its version. In
the R console, `R.version.string` prints it as well.

:::
